name: Scar tattooing / micropigmentation

lead: Scar tattooing, or micropigmentation, deposits pigment into scars, pale vitiligo patches or missing structures such as an areola so they look more like the surrounding skin. The color match shows once healed.

It belongs to the broader field of medical tattooing, and published information describes its history and uses, with evidence cited by Wikipedia consisting mainly of patient satisfaction reviews and general reviews of medical tattooing.

paras: A tattoo device places pigment in the dermis in a realistic style meant to imitate normal skin color. For scars, people may instead choose a decorative design that covers the area.

General tattoo risks include infection and allergic reactions. Wikipedia notes diabetes can impair wound healing, so timing and location may need care. Pigment is semi-permanent, and matching skin tone can be difficult.

angle.text: Micropigmentation places skin-toned pigment into scars or pale patches so they blend with the surrounding skin, and the match is visible once healed. It is used after surgery and for vitiligo, and appears among scar procedures in looksmaxxing discussions.

lead: Scar tattooing, also called micropigmentation, deposits skin-toned pigment into a scar or pale patch so the area blends with the surrounding skin. It is a form of medical tattooing, which aims to hide a condition or the result of its treatment, usually in a realistic style.[1] People use it to make surgical scars, vitiligo patches and missing areolas less noticeable, and the effect is an evener-looking skin surface without further surgery.[1][2]

A dermatology review describes micropigmentation as a semi-permanent camouflage technique used for stable vitiligo, for alopecia (including androgenetic alopecia and stable alopecia areata) and for semi-permanent makeup, and notes that knowledge of the indication and of colour theory matters for a natural-looking result.[2] The same family of methods includes scalp micropigmentation, where pigment dots imitate closely cut hair, and microblading, used to restore eyebrows lost to alopecia or trichotillomania.[1][3][4]

Within looksmaxxing discussion the method appears among non-surgical options for concealing scars and hair-transplant marks. Published information consists largely of clinical reviews, case reports and patient-satisfaction summaries rather than controlled comparisons.

paras: Medical tattoos are cosmetic tattoos meant to hide a condition or the results of its treatment, usually in a realistic style. For scars, people may alternatively choose a decorative cover-up design.[1] The technique is described in dermatology literature as novel and relatively easy to learn, relying on colour theory to choose pigments that approximate the surrounding skin.[2]

Documented uses include covering scars and simulating fingernails, reducing the visibility of vitiligo patches, and replacing a removed areola or filling pigment loss after free nipple grafts following mastectomy, reconstruction, breast reduction or chest masculinization.[1] Related microblading restores eyebrows lost to alopecia or trichotillomania.[1]

A 2023 review lists stable vitiligo, androgenetic alopecia, stable alopecia areata and semi-permanent makeup as the main dermatological indications.[2] Scalp micropigmentation, a close relative, places pigment between follicles in a stippling pattern that resembles closely cut hair, and is used to conceal hair loss.[3] Wikipedia's overview adds that it can also conceal hair-transplant scars and the marks of burns on the scalp, and that a course often takes several sessions.[4]

Wikipedia reports that in 1835 the German doctor Pauli tattooed skin lesions including nevi with mercury sulfide and white lead, and that lip scars were tattooed with cinnabar starting in 1911.[1] A 1996 article in Annals of Plastic Surgery titled Micropigmentation reflects the technique's place in plastic-surgery literature by the late twentieth century.[5]

Wikipedia's medical tattoo overview notes that diabetes can impair wound healing, so location and timing of a medical tattoo may need care in people with diabetes.[1] General tattoo considerations such as infection and allergy to ink apply, and practitioners of scalp micropigmentation may patch-test for ink allergy.[4] Pigment is semi-permanent, and matching it to skin tone is described as depending on the practitioner's colour skills.[2] Scalp pigment can be removed with laser treatment.[4]

No controlled trials of scar tattooing as such were found. The literature consists of narrative reviews and case reports: a 2023 review of micropigmentation indications,[2] a 2022 case report correlating scalp micropigmentation findings on trichoscopy and histopathology,[3] and a 1996 plastic surgery article.[5] Wikipedia cites a 2021 systematic review of patient satisfaction with medical tattooing and earlier reviews without summarising their findings.[1] A registered trial (NCT04046679) examines a bleomycin infusion technique to repigment achromic scars; it is a different method from tattooing.[6]
